title: When Inquiry Learning Is Malpractice Date Published: June 3, 2026 Original URL: https://fillingthepail.substack.com
author: Greg Ashman
summary: Ashman argues that inquiry learning is not merely inferior to explicit teaching in many contexts but constitutes genuine malpractice when used as the primary method for novice learners — students who have not yet acquired the knowledge base needed to benefit from open-ended investigation. A key complication is definitional drift: inquiry advocates increasingly redefine 'explicit teaching' to refer only to brief, non-interactive explanation, so they can then claim inquiry is compatible with it, obscuring decades of process-product research showing extended, interactive explicit teaching outperforms inquiry. Ashman's own definition of explicit teaching encompasses the full arc from clear explanation and worked examples through to complex student-generated products — it is not just the explanation phase that distinguishes his position. A novice learner is not someone who knows nothing, but simply someone who doesn't yet know what the teacher is trying to teach — making novice status relative to specific learning objectives rather than global knowledge. There is a defensible, narrow role for inquiry: as a complex culminating task after students have gained relative expertise, to practice and consolidate what has already been taught explicitly. The Australian Federal Government's own education website defines inquiry as 'reversing the order of learning' by presenting problems before answers — Ashman argues this specific reversal is the practice the evidence consistently shows to be ineffective for novices.
points: The 'false choice' framing deployed by inquiry advocates is not neutral: below the surface, it almost always conceals a preference for inquiry, which is why Ashman insists on naming when and for whom each method is appropriate rather than simply calling for 'balance'.

The definitional erosion of 'explicit teaching' — now being redefined to mean any short burst of explanation — is a deliberate strategy that severs the term from its evidence base (process-product research stretching back to the 1960s), forcing proponents to keep finding new language for the same approach.

Ashman's tiebreaker test for when inquiry is legitimate: if the student already has relative expertise in the content area, open-ended tasks can serve to practice, consolidate, and apply that knowledge — even if they probably won't produce substantial new learning.

Labelling explicit teaching a 'pedagogy of poverty' (as a recent Australian position paper did) is precisely the kind of ideologically-loaded characterisation that Ashman identifies as a rhetorical move to avoid engaging with the actual evidence.

The practical implication for teachers is simpler than the debate suggests: teach explicitly first, ensure novice learners have knowledge in place, and only then assign open-ended tasks that require them to apply and extend that knowledge.
quotes: There is an ongoing debate about the relative merits of explicit teaching and inquiry learning. One side usually frames this as a false choice, arguing that both methods are useful and valid, usually without specifying what factors a teacher should consider before choosing one method or the other at a particular point in time.

The other side of this debate — to which I belong — argues that inquiry-style activities should only come after a critical mass of knowledge has been taught explicitly. We therefore advocate explicit teaching as the primary strategy for novice learners.

What is a novice learner? It is not a student who knows nothing at all; it is simply a student who does not yet know the things the teacher is seeking to teach them. It is worth noting that to make such an assessment, a teacher must therefore have a clear learning objective.

When I refer to explicit teaching, I mean an entire process that starts with fully explaining concepts and procedures but that ends with students — eventually — creating complex products such as essays or artworks, or tackling challenging mathematics problems.

'Inquiry-based learning is an education approach that focuses on investigation and problem-solving. Inquiry-based learning is different from traditional approaches because it reverses the order of learning. Instead of presenting information, or 'the answer', up-front, teachers start with a range of scenarios, questions and problems for students to navigate.'

Unfortunately, the same process of erosion seems to now be happening to my preferred term. For example, some commentators appear to believe that explicit teaching refers to any period of teacher explanation or exposition, no matter how short and regardless of whether or not it is interactive.
